analysis.one_liner: Exempts premium cigars from FDA regulation and from FDA user fees.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 59 cosponsors from both parties but never moved past a House subcommittee, and it died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would change federal food and drug law so that traditional large and premium cigars — hand-rolled cigars, or a narrow machine-made category with a leaf wrapper — are not covered by the FDA's tobacco rules. It would also block the FDA from writing any regulations on these cigars and would exclude them from the user fees that fund FDA tobacco oversight.
analysis.who_benefits: Premium cigar manufacturers, importers, and retail shops, including small handmade-cigar businesses and lounges. They would avoid FDA user fees and compliance costs, and would face no risk of future FDA rules on warnings, ingredients, or manufacturing for these products.

how_it_helps.text: The bill exempts traditional large and premium cigars from the FDA's tobacco chapter of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act and states that nothing in that chapter gives the Health Secretary authority to regulate any matter involving these cigars.
It excludes premium cigars from FDA user fees, so manufacturers and importers would no longer pay the charges that fund FDA tobacco oversight.

The exemption is targeted: it covers cigars wrapped in 100% leaf tobacco with no filter, tip, or flavor additive, hand-rolled or (for US-made cigars) laid by hand onto a single bunching machine, and it does not include cigarettes or little cigars.

analysis.who_pays: The public, and especially cigar users, who would get no FDA-mandated health warnings, ingredient disclosure, or manufacturing oversight for a tobacco product, and no fee-funded FDA capacity to review these cigars' risks.
analysis.who_pays_short: Cigar users and the broader public

drawbacks.text: The bill removes FDA authority — including health warnings and ingredient and manufacturing requirements — over cigars, which are tobacco products that carry cancer and heart disease risks; the exemption is permanent and blocks any future FDA rulemaking for these cigars.

With premium cigars carved out of FDA user fees, the cost of overseeing the remaining tobacco market shifts elsewhere, and a category of addictive products sits outside the same oversight applied to cigarettes.

An honest supporter would acknowledge that the bill prioritizes the business costs of regulation for a niche industry over the public-health rationale for applying one tobacco framework to all tobacco products; the counterargument is that hand-made premium cigars are an artisanal small business and are used differently from cigarettes, so one-size-fits-all FDA rules are a poor fit.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but narrow: saving small cigar makers and shops compliance costs and user fees. The cost is leaving an addictive, cancer-causing tobacco category permanently outside FDA warnings, disclosure, and rulemaking authority. For a public-health agency's framework, a permanent blanket exemption for a whole product class is a large carve-out to justify with a jobs argument, and the bill offered no substitute safeguards.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Health Subcommittee, never received a hearing or a vote, and expired when the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Kathy Castor introduced the bill on June 17, 2021, joining Rep. Bill Posey as the original Republican co-sponsor, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day.
The next day it was referred to the committee's Health Subcommittee, where the action record ends.
The bill attracted 59 cosponsors — 49 Republicans and 10 Democrats — but the committee never took it up, and the bill received no floor vote before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the FDA's existing authority over premium cigars — including its rules and user fees — stayed in place, so the outcome favored public-health oversight over the cigar industry, which continued to bear regulation it had sought to escape.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: FDA oversight stayed; cigar makers kept paying

sides.party_line_note: The cosponsor list was 49 Republicans and 10 Democrats, with a Florida Democrat leading and a Florida Republican as original co-sponsor, but the opposition was inaction rather than a recorded vote.

industries.note: The bill would have freed them from FDA user fees and any FDA rulemaking — health warnings, ingredient disclosure, manufacturing standards — for their product. Their gain is the public's loss of oversight over an addictive tobacco product.

industries.industry: Small cigar retailers and cigar lounges
industries.note: The bill's stated purpose is protecting small businesses that sell and distribute traditional cigars, which would have benefited from the same exemption from federal tobacco regulation and fees.
